Its plot is propelled by soap-operatic twists (I’m surprised hysterical blindness didn’t come into play), the stupidity of the characters (one character parks just outside his torture chamber in a pick-up with his full name emblazoned on the door), and insultingly stupid writing (too many examples to even begin...and the police work is absurd ): no one is redeemable here and I hate them all. Yeah yeah, it pays trivial lip service to moral commentary by painting a bleak portrait of the modern condition blah blah blah, but its gross insensitivity renders it crap. And at 2.5 hours, it’s galling crap.

Hard to say something about it because I really liked some of the aspects about it: the performances which are great, the premise which is very interesting, the cast is talented and the beginning had potencial but along the way the movie just falls apart, things just don't make much sense. Keller doesn't stop to think that a mentally disable guy that has a 10 IQ and a mind of a child is the prime suspect of what happened with his daughter, but that doesn't have any logic since the police already confirmed after interrogating the guy that he is innocent, the guy also doesn't seem to be able to do anything other than just mumbling some nonsense that only him understand. He is not responsible for the crime commited against those two families but the MC keeps brutalizing and destroying him anyway, making a victim of kidnapp and abuse to be kidnapped and abused again is terrible. He is just a kid, functionally. But Keller doesn't care anyway and his methods couldn't help him to do shit in the whole process. The truth was discovered by detective Loki without any of Keller's actions and when Loki got to the place was almost too late. Fortunately, he was able to save Keller's girl, which also doesn't make any sense since he couldn't even see straight while driving under a heavy rain. Feels forced and hard to believe someone in that situation was able to save another person while being injured and with almost no time at all. Girls were both saved without any permanent scars or wounds, which also is unbelievable and stupid, since the serial killer abused and killer so many other kids before. Why those two were already alive and well after days being dissapeared? Why maintain them well and with life? How keeping them well that long around was a good idea? Nothing makes much sense. 0 internal logic and the whole story pushes forward the idea of "the end justifies the means", a dangerous, problematic and toxic message to the audience and the public in general. The guy tortured a kid to find his own kid while praying to God, how hypocrital is he? How insane is the director? Not right make a character like Alex suffer what he had to endure and then be saved off-screen, after being explicited tortured for so much time. Could you do the same in his place? Would you have the guts to do what is "necessary" for save who you love? Whatever it takes can cost another life, can take you push your own limits, but the movie the never makes you criticize the dark and violent things the protagonist does, it actually makes you empathize with the violent father more than with the victim of all the torture and abuse. The film wasn't written well enough to make you care for all the victims, only with a portion of them, a couple of kids you know nothing while the ones that suffered the most are just treated as the monsters. Really a shame. Could have been much better in so many ways. The more I think about the less I like it. It's only a fine movie. Appreciated to see Jackman and Gyllenhaal acting together, not appreciated as how mentally ill people are portrayed and how violence and tortured are excused as "the only way" to save someone else, when the victim isn't even the real criminal. I feel more bad about Alex than I feel about that two girls. Sorry. And what was that ambigous ending? 2 hours and a half to make a open finale? Seriously? This is so disrespecful and stupid with the audience. Open endings can work with some movies but this piece of media is definitely NOT one of them. The real prisoners are my expectations that got locked away from a true good experience. And they won't be free. 4 out of 10. 2 ☆☆

Bro, I am straight-up not having a good time. Kind of wanted to barf more than once! Keller’s torture of Alex shows textbook domestic abuse tactics. He blames Alex for “making” him do this, and he uses his religious beliefs as a shield for his actions, even praying before and after torturing Alex. It’s terrifying, and it makes me worried for his wife and children. Parts of this reminded me of The Vanishing to a distracting degree. This probably isn’t the movie’s fault, but I found the name Alex Jones distracting too. I’m not sure how much of a following the real-life Alex Jones had at the time of the film’s release, but I couldn’t hear the name without thinking about him. I wish the daughters’ mothers had more to do. I really liked the scene of Nancy questioning Alex and later deciding that she will not participate in Keller’s interrogation of him but will not stop him either, and it’s wasted potential that we see so little of her after that. Some of the themes feel half-baked too. There are hints of commentary on religion turning people violent, but it only tiptoes around that without really delving into it. I feel similarly about the themes of child abuse. I like a depressing movie, even the occasional mean movie that gives you glimmers of hope only to dash it. But this was too mean-spirited even for me, and I wish that some things were explored in more depth. I guess it ultimately left me thinking “But what is the point?”

Lived up to my expectations. Denis Villeneuve’s Prisoners is a very well crafted thriller that undoubtedly needs to be watched at night to fit the vibe of the movie. Crime thrillers are one of my favourite movie genres so i was bound to enjoy this. Hugh Jackman in my opinion has his best ever performance in this film. His character Keller Dover is the father of one of the kidnapped children and as the movie goes along, day by day you can see his rage increase and his reliance on humanity fades. In many scenes you can hear his voice break and your dragged into his broken psyche. This performance was stellar. Jake Gyllenhaal played Detective Loki, a detective who boasts his history of solving every crime he has previously met. However the one he is about to tackle, challenges and eats away at his mind. In many ways his mind is imprisoned in the maze of the case mystery. Paul Dano plays the kidnapper suspect and watching this film, it makes absolute sense why Dano was chosen to play the Riddler. Such a chilling and subtle creepiness he brings to the screen. David Dastmalchian was a suprise addition to the cast and he was a treat to see. He aswell fit the creepy and dark vibe of his character. The final third of the film was goddamn great. A plot twist that really makes you locked in on what happens next. And question what you previously watched. Bravo Denis Villeneuve 👏

Un film qui t'attrape à la gorge dès les premières minutes et ne desserre jamais l'étau, au point que le silence qui suit le générique dit probablement plus que n'importe quelle critique écrite après coup. Villeneuve construit une ambiance anxiogène qui colle à la peau, chaque plan semble porter le poids du désespoir, et cette descente aux enfers parallèle, Jackman rongé par une rage paternelle incontrôlable, Gyllenhaal miné par l'impuissance méthodique de l'enquête, fonctionne parce qu'on ne se contente pas de comprendre leur effondrement, on le ressent physiquement à leurs côtés. La scène de la salle de bain reste un modèle de malaise, cette violence qui explose contre un homme visiblement inapte et manipulé n'est jamais gratuite, elle incarne au contraire toute l'horreur de la vengeance aveugle, celle qui frappe sans discernement quand l'espoir a disparu. Un thriller qui ne cherche jamais le twist facile, mais la vérité la plus dérangeante possible sur ce que le désespoir peut faire d'un homme.

This film might be one of my most favourite films of all time. It is so creative. The movie follows a father whom is played by Hugh Jackman, the film is centred around his daughter and her friend being kidnapped/going missing. He takes matters into his own hands to find her or gather any information/evidence on her whereabouts so he gets closer to figuring out what happened to her. Detective Loki, played by Jake Gyllenhaal, is the main detective who is put on this case. Each performance in this film is all done extremely well. There’s so much depth and meaning in each and every character. This might be one of Hugh Jackman and Paul Dano’s best performances. The story is also very interesting and well written. “Prisoners” is highly praised feature that portrays the concept of a profoundly unsettling, emotional, and suspenseful investigation of a missing child in such an incredible and distinctive way. It portrays the anger and rage of a dad who is just trying to find his daughter and the feared feeling towards the suspected with unique story telling. It reveals the plot twist in a way that is quite unpredictable and many first-time watchers would not be able to figure out. The acting from each actor/actress is in done in an oscar worthy performance. Hugh Jackman absolutely stands out in this film because of how well he shows the realistic anger of a parent whose is daughter was kidnapped and he’s just carrying the pain of almost losing a child. Paul Dano feels more and more unsettling everytime he’s on screen because of how insane his character is and the brilliant performance he put on as a truly mind-twisted antagonist. The pacing is very important in this film and it really shows it with how well directed this film is. It’s a film that doesn’t necessarily have any confusing scenes and is easily understood. In terms of violence and gore in this film, there’s more than a few scenes that contain some gore but it actually makes sense and it’s properly placed. The cinematography stays true to the plot and every scene is well filmed. The ending itself is a major plot twist that is understandable because it gives the viewers a sense of what had happened after the film’s ending. Denis Villeneuve did quite well with the directing of this film. I have watched this film more than once and it just gets better after every rewatch.
